deckTitle: The Hand-Crank: Why Startups Need a Manual Start

direction.conceit: Hand-cranking an old car engine. The startup is a motor that won't start by itself. The founder's arm does the cold, hard work of turning it over, and once it catches, it runs on its own power.
direction.motif: A crank handle and an engine tachometer. Every slide shows the RPM needle somewhere between 'dead cold' and 'running on its own', with a marked ignition line. The reader always knows how far the engine is from catching, and whether a hand is still needed on the crank.
direction.arc: Startups don't start themselves → starting and running are two different jobs → the crank is recruiting users by hand → founders skip it because small numbers look like nothing → compounding shows they aren't → before it catches, the engine can stall → so judge potential, not current size → planes need engines, cannonballs fall → a test for plans with no effort → the forms the crank takes → being small is why you can turn it → an idea is a pair: the engine plus the crank.

slides.title: The big idea: startups don't start themselves

intent.title: The big idea: startups don't start themselves
intent.claim: Startups take off because founders make them take off. They do not take off just because the product is good.
intent.mechanism: A founder's arm applies force to a crank. The engine (the startup) turns over but does not fire on its own. Only after enough cranking does it catch, and then it runs without the arm. Without the arm, nothing happens, however good the engine is.
intent.aha: The mousetrap myth pictures the engine starting on its own. The picture shows an arm is required.
intent.resting: An old car engine with a crank handle at the front and a founder's hand on it. A tachometer reads near 'dead cold', with the ignition line marked well above the needle. A caption contrasts the myth ('build a better mousetrap and they come') with the reality ('someone has to turn the crank').

intent.title: Two separate jobs
intent.claim: Starting a startup and keeping it running are two separate jobs. The first one is manual, and it ends at a threshold.
intent.mechanism: Cranking adds RPM. Below the ignition line, RPM decays back to zero as soon as cranking stops. Above it, the engine sustains its own RPM and the crank is no longer needed. The input is the founder's effort. The relation is the threshold. The output is self-sustaining motion, or a fall back to cold.
intent.operate: The reader turns the crank (presses or drags to add turns) and can let go at any moment.
intent.changes: The tachometer needle rises with each turn. If released below the ignition line, it sinks back to cold. Once past the line, the engine catches, the crank arm drops away, and the needle holds steady in the 'running on its own' zone.
intent.aha: Letting go just short of the line sends the needle all the way back to zero. Crossing it makes the arm unnecessary. These are two different jobs, and the first one doesn't partly count.
intent.resting: Two labeled zones on the tachometer: 'Starting: your arm' below the ignition line and 'Running: its own power' above it. The needle is cold and a ghost trace shows one failed attempt that sank back. This reads alone as: effort below the line is lost if you stop, and effort past it is no longer needed.

claim_at_rest.read_claim: Getting growth started and keeping it going are two different jobs: founders first have to push it by hand, with effort that doesn't scale, until it passes an ignition threshold where it can run on its own, so don't expect self-sustaining growth to start by itself.

intent.title: What turning the crank looks like
intent.claim: Turning the crank mostly means recruiting users one at a time, in person, and finishing the setup for them on the spot.
intent.mechanism: Two paths from the same 'yes, I'll try it'. In the diffident path, the founder sends a link, and the user has to remember, open it and set things up alone, so each step can lose them. In the Collison path, the founder says 'give me your laptop', and the yes becomes an installed user right there. The output is how many yeses become actual users.
intent.aha: Even after the user says yes, the link path still leaves room to lose them. The Collison installation turns the yes straight into a running user.
intent.resting: Two columns from one 'Will you try it?' / 'Yes'. Left, 'We'll send you a link': a path with several gaps where the user can drop off. Right, 'Right then, give me your laptop': one step straight to a working setup. Stripe is labeled on the right, with a note that even Stripe, solving an urgent problem, didn't wait.

claim_at_rest.read_claim: Ten people say yes to the same offer. If you just send them a link, only about 3 end up as running users, because people forget, put it off or get stuck on setup. If the founder sets it up for them on the spot, the way the Collisons did at Stripe, all 10 end up as running users.

items.q: What does the car-engine crank metaphor say about how startups take off?
items.ref: Startups don't usually take off on their own. The founders have to push them through a separate, laborious start-up phase, like hand-cranking an engine, and after that the engine keeps running by itself.
items.answer: Startups don't start themselves: like a car before electric starters, founders have to turn the crank by hand, which is a separate, manual, tiring job. Once the engine catches, it keeps running on its own.
items.why: Gets the key idea: founders push the startup through a separate, hand-cranked start-up phase, and after that it runs on its own.

items.q: Why does the essay argue that recruiting users one by one is worth it even though the numbers seem tiny at first?
items.ref: Because of compound growth. If you keep up a steady weekly growth rate like 10%, small absolute gains build into huge numbers (about 14,000 users after one year and 2 million after two), so manual recruiting can get you to scale.
items.answer: Small numbers aren't small because growth compounds. At 10% a week, 100 users become 110, then about 14,000 in a year and about 2 million in two years, so 10 hand-recruited users can be that 10% weekly growth. Thinking '10 users can't be how the big ones started' is described as a factual error about how growth works.
items.why: Explains compound growth at 10% a week, with the matching figures (about 14,000 users in a year, 2 million in two).

items.q: What mistake do inexperienced founders and investors make when they judge early startups, and what question should they ask instead?
items.ref: They judge fragile, larval startups by the standards of established companies and dismiss them. Instead they should ask how big the company could get if the founders did the right things.
items.answer: They judge a tiny startup by an established company's standards and ask 'Is this taking over the world yet?', which leads to quitting too early. They should ask 'How big could this get if the founders did the right things?'
items.why: Names both the mistake (judging by established-company standards) and the better question (how big could this get).

items.q: How can a small startup give better customer service than a big company, and why do founders often fail to see this?
items.ref: Being small lets founders give personal attention that big companies can't, like hand-written thank-you notes. Founders miss this because their standards for service were set by the big companies they've been customers of, and because engineers aren't trained in customer service.
items.answer: Being tiny lets a startup give attention no big company can, such as a handwritten note, and that attention makes up for a buggy, unfinished product so the total user experience beats the giant's. The deck doesn't really say why founders miss this, though it suggests they see their small numbers as a weakness.
items.why: Covers how being small allows personal attention, but leaves out why founders miss it (standards set by big companies, engineers not trained in customer service).

items.q: In a startup's early months, how does the meaning of 'insanely great' shift, and why does over-engaging with users improve the product?
items.ref: What should be insanely great is the experience of being a user, not the product, so attentiveness can make up for a buggy, incomplete product. Engaging directly with early users also gives the best feedback, which drives the iteration that makes the product good.
items.answer: The deck doesn't show how the meaning of 'insanely great' shifts. It only says that attention makes up for a buggy, unfinished product, and that talking to users gives you the best feedback you'll ever have, which flows back into the product.
items.why: Gets attention making up for a buggy product and the feedback loop, but doesn't say the shift is to the user experience rather than the product.

items.q: Why might a startup deliberately start in a narrow market, as Facebook did with Harvard?
items.ref: Like keeping a fire contained so it gets hot, a narrow market lets you reach critical mass quickly because the users feel the product is really for them. You can then expand from there.
items.answer: Starting narrow, with Harvard students only, lets a startup reach critical mass in a small group instead of having to reach it across a whole market.
items.why: Gets reaching critical mass in a small group, but leaves out users feeling the product is for them and expanding from there.

items.q: What benefits come from doing things manually that you plan to automate later, or from building hardware yourself, as Meraki and Pebble did?
items.ref: It lets you launch faster and avoid obstacles like large minimum factory orders. You also learn exactly what to build or automate, and in hardware you can tweak the design faster, because you've done the work yourself.
items.answer: The deck doesn't mention Meraki. It says Pebble built its first several hundred watches by hand instead of placing a factory order (minimum several hundred thousand dollars), and Stripe set up 'instant' accounts manually instead of waiting for automation that didn't exist yet: a person does by hand what the system can't do yet.
items.why: Covers launching faster and avoiding minimum factory orders, but leaves out learning what to build or automate and tweaking designs faster.

items.q: Why does the essay reject the 'Big Launch' and big-company partnerships, and what does it mean to think of startup ideas as vectors rather than scalars?
items.ref: Startups are like powered aircraft, not projectiles: success depends on sustained effort and on how happy you make your first users, not on initial velocity, and strategies that skip the effort are suspect. A startup idea should be seen as a pair: what you'll build plus the unscalable things you'll do to get started, and ideally those things become a permanent part of the company's DNA.
items.answer: A big launch or partnership is like a cannonball: one blast, then it falls, whereas a startup needs its own engine running all the time, a core group of happy users who drive growth. Treating an idea as a vector means it is a pair, what you'll build plus how you'll hand-start it, and the habits from that hand-start stay in the company as it grows.
items.why: Gets the projectile-vs-engine contrast (sustained effort, happy users) and the idea as a pair (what you build plus unscalable start-up work) that stays in the company's DNA.
